Conform Ducky code to SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The Ducky and chore classes break several rules of the SE-EDU Java
coding standard: the class name is lower-case, many braces and
operators lack surrounding spaces, two lines exceed the length
limit, and the public types and methods have no Javadoc. Two
compiled .class files are tracked by mistake as well.

Let's bring the Java tree in line with the standard:

- Rename class chore to Chore (PascalCase) and rename the file to
  match; update every reference in Ducky.
- Add a space before opening braces and around binary operators,
  and drop the space between a method name and its parenthesis.
- Wrap the two over-long println statements before the + operator.
- Replace the bare array size 100 with a named constant MAX_CHORES.
- Add class and method Javadoc, and correct a stale comment that
  referred to a "bye" command and to echoing input.
- Stop tracking Ducky.class and chore.class, and ignore *.class.

No behaviour change: command output is identical and the code
compiles on Java 25.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add mandatory SE-EDU Java coding standard skill
commitResults.messageBody:
The project has no written Java style rules, so naming, formatting,
and documentation have drifted across the code base.

Let's adopt the SE-EDU Java coding standard (Basic + Intermediate):

- Add the seedu-java-coding-standard skill, which captures the rules
  for naming, layout, statements, and Javadoc plus a pre-commit
  checklist.
- Require the skill from a new mandatory section in AGENTS.md so it
  is applied to all Java work, new and existing.
- Override one rule by project decision: comments and Javadoc use
  British spelling, not the American spelling the standard specifies.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level 4, did the tasks variations using inheritance
Extract command handlers out of Ducky.main
commitResults.messageBody:
The main method reads a command line, then decides what to do, parses
the arguments, mutates the chore list, and formats the output all in one
place. At roughly a hundred lines with a long chain of if blocks, it
mixes several levels of abstraction and forces a reader to scan the
whole method to find any single command's behaviour.

Move each command's logic into its own named method (printChores,
markChore, unmarkChore, addToDo, addDeadline, addEvent) and pull the
shared deadline/event confirmation into printAddedChore. The greeting
banner moves into printIntroduction. The main loop now reads as a plain
dispatch table: match the command word, delegate, repeat.

The add handlers return the updated chore count so that main keeps
ownership of the loop state instead of relying on a shared mutable
field. Behaviour and all user-facing text are unchanged; this is a
pure structural refactoring verified by running the sample commands.

Also rename the local variables chorelist and counter to chores and
choreCount to match the coding standard (plural name for a collection,
camelCase throughout) now that they are passed across method
boundaries and need to read clearly.

commitResults.messageTitle: Derive command-argument offsets from the keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
Each command handler slices the argument off the input line with a bare
number: input.substring(5) after "mark ", substring(9) after
"deadline ", and so on. The number has no visible connection to the
word it skips, so a reader has to count characters to check it, and it
silently goes wrong if the keyword in the matching startsWith call is
ever changed without updating the offset.

Replace the literal with input.substring("mark".length()) and the like.
The keyword stays spelled out in the code, which reads naturally and
matches what the user types, but the offset is now computed from that
same word instead of being a separate constant to keep in sync. The
trailing trim() still strips the separating space, so behaviour is
unchanged; verified with the sample commands.

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject unrecognised commands instead of ignoring them
commitResults.messageBody:
The command dispatch chain ends after the "event" branch with no final
else, so any line that matches none of the known commands falls through
in silence. A user who mistypes a command, or expects a command Ducky
does not have, gets no feedback and cannot tell whether the input was
accepted.

Add a closing else branch that echoes the unrecognised input and lists
the commands Ducky understands. This follows the guideline that a
decision chain should always handle the default case rather than assume
the remaining inputs are impossible.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename Deadlines and Events to singular nouns
commitResults.messageBody:
The subclasses of Chore are named Deadlines and Events, but each
instance represents exactly one deadline or one event, not a
collection. The plural reads as if the class were a list type and is
inconsistent with the other chore class, ToDo, which is singular.

Rename the classes and their constructors to Deadline and Event, and
update the two call sites in Ducky. A class name should be a noun that
describes a single instance; the plural form is reserved for
collections.

commitResults.messageTitle: Format the event description like the deadline one
commitResults.messageBody:
Event.getDescription() concatenates its suffix directly onto the
description with no separating space, producing "meeting(from: ...)",
while Deadline.getDescription() produces "return book (by: ...)". The
inconsistent spacing looks like a typo in the list output.

Add the leading space so both chore types render as
"<description> (<details>)". While on this line, space the concatenation
operators and drop the stray space before the semicolon to match the
coding standard.

commitResults.messageTitle: Conform chore classes to the SE-EDU coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The Chore hierarchy has several small standard violations: opening
braces stuck to the class and method names without a space, overriding
methods with no @Override annotation, a bare "//" comment where Javadoc
belongs, missing Javadoc on public classes, constructors and non-trivial
methods, and stray blank lines.

Add the missing spaces and @Override annotations, replace the comment on
Chore.getTypeIcon() with a proper Javadoc block, and document each
class, constructor and overridden method. No behaviour changes; the
sample commands produce the same output.

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove duplicate "chore added" line in addToDo
commitResults.messageBody:
addToDo prints "QUACKDDING: <description>" and then calls
printAddedChore, which prints its own "QUACKDDING! I've added this
chore:" banner followed by the same description. Every "todo" command
therefore shows the chore twice, while "deadline" and "event" show it
once via printAddedChore alone.

The leftover line predates printAddedChore's extraction and was never
removed once the shared helper took over announcing added chores.

Let's delete the leftover line so addToDo matches addDeadline and
addEvent, giving every add command one consistent confirmation
message.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract ChoreList to own chore storage
commitResults.messageBody:
Ducky.main holds the chores array and choreCount directly, and every
add/mark/print helper has to receive both and, for the add helpers,
manually return the updated count. This spreads storage bookkeeping
across the UI-parsing class instead of keeping it in one place, and
it caps storage at a hardcoded MAX_CHORES = 100 with no bounds check,
so a 101st chore would throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Let's extract a ChoreList class that owns the chores and exposes
add/get/size. Ducky now holds a single ChoreList and no longer threads
choreCount through method calls, and the backing ArrayList removes the
fixed-capacity limit.

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject invalid mark/unmark ranks instead of crashing
commitResults.messageBody:
markChore and unmarkChore parse the rank with Integer.parseInt and
index straight into the chore list. A non-numeric rank throws
NumberFormatException, and a rank of 0 or one beyond the list size
throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, crashing Ducky instead of reporting
the mistake.

Let's add a shared parseChoreIndex helper that both commands use: it
parses the rank, checks it against the list bounds, and prints a
QUACK?! message and returns -1 on failure instead of letting the
exception propagate. Sharing the helper also removes the near-duplicate
parsing logic that markChore and unmarkChore previously had.
